title: Inch Fractions and Decimals: A Reference Chart
h1: Inch fractions and decimals — the workshop cheat sheet
description: A 3/16 drill is 0.1875 in = 4.7625 mm. Here is the full fraction-to-decimal-to-mm table, and why fractional inches survive in modern shops.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against ANSI B94.11M drill sizes

hero: Every 64th of an inch has an exact decimal and an exact millimetre value. Once memorised, they let you read any inch drawing without a calculator.
body: Fractional inches survive because drills, taps, wrenches and structural bolts are still manufactured to fractional sizes. A modern machinist reads 3/8-16 UNC as automatically as 10-32 metric. This is the reference table that makes it fluent.

Every fraction n/64 in has an exact terminating decimal because 64 is a power of 2, and 25.4 mm converts every one to an exact decimal in mm too. There is no rounding in the fraction system — the imprecision only enters when someone rounds to two decimal places on a drawing.

US drill sets step by 1/64 up to 1/2, then by 1/32. A 'letter drill' set fills in between fractional sizes with 26 letters (A = 0.234 in through Z = 0.413 in). A 'number drill' set covers below 1/4 in with 80 sizes. Metric equivalents rarely land within 0.1 mm of a fractional size, which is why a US shop keeps both drill cabinets.

A 3/8-16 UNC tap needs a tap drill of about 5/16 in = 0.3125 in = 7.938 mm. The closest metric drill (8 mm = 0.315 in) is 0.062 mm larger — enough to reduce thread engagement from 75% to about 68%, which is still functional but marginally weaker. In critical joints, use the fractional drill.
n/64 inch × 0.396875 = mm. n/16 inch × 1.5875 = mm. Every fractional inch has an exact mm equivalent — the only rounding in imperial machining is voluntary.

faqs.a: Historical binary halving with dividers. A machinist can bisect a line by eye to 1/64, but not to 1/100.
In consumer electronics and cars, yes. In US construction and aerospace, fractional-inch bolts still dominate.

faqs.q: What is a 'plus one' fractional size?
faqs.a: One 64th above the nominal. A 3/8+1 drill is 25/64 in = 0.3906 in — used for clearance holes where a plain 3/8 is too tight.
